facts.text: The opening crawl spells it "Hoards of armored robots" when it should be "hordes". The typo is famous enough that it's pointed out in write-ups of the film.
Co-writer Brian Hannant got the idea while working on Mad Max 2 (The Road Warrior), when he fell for the Wilpena Pound rock formation in South Australia. He built the script around it.
The film's budget was about A$8 million. Director Brian Hannant said it was raised in two days, with roughly $1 million of it lost to brokers.
Dean Stockwell, who plays the city's leader Boss, was Oscar-nominated for Best Supporting Actor for Married to the Mob (1988), the year after this Australian sci-fi flop opened.
The original script, called Time Rider, had just ONE Jen-Diki monster, with $150,000 set aside to make it work. A producer demanded hordes of robots, but the budget didn't grow.

The effects shots were filmed using a blue-screen rear-projection rig designed by Douglas Trumbull (2001, Blade Runner), installed in an old Adelaide cinema. The crew learned rotoscoping for the film.
Wilpena Pound, the rock formation that inspired the script (its Aboriginal name Ikara means "meeting place"), survives in the final cut only as one aerial establishing shot.
Look at the scrolling sign board around now. Fans spot C-3PO on it, possibly a nod to star Carrie Fisher, who played Princess Leia opposite Anthony Daniels' C-3PO in Star Wars.
Carrie Fisher was Princess Leia in Star Wars. The villains here are the Jen-Diki, a name that looks suspiciously like "Jedi" with extra letters added.
Carrie Fisher and Dean Stockwell were the only American actors in this Australian production. They were brought in to add international marquee value.
The script's prospectus asked for "Scott Glenn or equivalent", a mature sci-fi action actor. Hemdale cast boyish Tom Burlinson as Ballard instead, which co-writer John Baxter lamented.
Director Brian Hannant said that Hemdale, the film's financier, handed him a rewrite by an American writer eight weeks before shooting. Hannant called the replacement script "laughable".
The shoot was cut from a planned 13 weeks to 9. Director Brian Hannant later described the production as "like watching the Titanic going down".
Author Tony Ayres called this "Australia's first attempt at high-technology science fiction" in his book Australian Film 1978-1994.
Cinematographer Geoff Burton said the crew knew the limits: "we couldn't make anything really stylish." The anamorphic widescreen format helped hide the low budget.
Special effects supervisor Andrew Mason on this film later became an executive producer of The Matrix trilogy, according to the Australian Screen Online archive.
Hero Ballard may be named after sci-fi author J.G. Ballard. Fans also compare the Jen-Diki leader, Zuryk, to Davros from Doctor Who.
Composer Allan Zavod's score is keyboard-based rather than orchestral, and the end-credit song "This Time I Know" is sung by Angry Anderson, who is on the soundtrack.
Ballard being a feral child raised by nomads nods to The Road Warrior's Feral Kid. Director Brian Hannant co-wrote that film.
Producer Antony I. Ginnane was known for cutting script pages to control budgets, and kept pulling pages during the shoot. Director Brian Hannant said Hemdale wanted a Terminator-style hit.
Co-writer John Baxter said his Time Rider script was meant to open and close with a firefight at Hemdale's request. He joked that it explained the awkward opening of The Terminator.
Filming used the South Australian Film Corporation's soundstages at Hendon in Adelaide plus a deserted quarry outside the city. Mirage Effects handled the special effects.
Producer Antony I. Ginnane meant this to be the first of a ten-picture deal with Hemdale. When Hemdale pulled out, the other nine films were shelved.
Critic David Stratton said "an entire book could probably be written about The Time Guardian." Curator Richard Kuipers called it "one of the great missed opportunities of Australian cinema."
Richard Scheib of Moria gave it two stars. He called it "an efficient film but an unremarkable one", and noted the visible budget limits.
Filmink wrote that Tom Burlinson's performance as Ballard "killed his career as a leading man." He had starred in The Man from Snowy River (1982) and Phar Lap (1983).
The film came from Australia's 10BA tax-incentive boom. Critic David Stratton said it showed how deal-driven 10BA films could be undone: "the wrong producers, the wrong deals, the wrong budget".
The script was first sold to Chateau Productions, whom writer-director Brian Hannant described as "song pluggers who'd made commercials and documentaries" and decided to make a feature.
The TV playing as the mechanic calls the sheriff shows a clip from The Terminator. On some copies of this film the TV is blurred or cut out, likely over clip rights.
A full-size Jen-Diki armor suit from this film was reportedly for sale in a pop-culture shop in Tyabb, south of Melbourne, in the mid-2000s.
Director Brian Hannant quit during post-production after producer Antony I. Ginnane showed the unfinished cut to head office. Co-writer John Baxter said he left one step ahead of being fired.
Hannant left, so the film's editor shot some extra scenes. Author Tony Ayres wrote that the film was recut and partly reshot, and that Hannant disowns much of it.
It flopped. It failed to recoup its marketing costs, and Hemdale couldn't pay its A$4.8 million pre-sale. It agreed to pay a reduced A$2 million instead.
In the Philippines it was released as Spacetrap. Six Nintendo Family Computer consoles were raffled off during the first three days of release.
Filmink wrote that a film this wasteful makes Australian sci-fi harder, but "should have a bigger cult". It said Nikki Coghill is "genuinely charming amidst the carnage".
